nameStory: The Promethea Silkmoth gets its name from Prometheus, the Greek titan who stole fire from the gods to give to humans. Just as Prometheus brought light to humanity, this moth emerges from its winter cocoon to bring beauty to our spring forests. It's also called the spicebush silkmoth after one of its favorite host plants.
description: The Promethea Silkmoth is one of New England's most striking giant silk moths, with a wingspan that can reach 4 inches across. Males are dramatically different from females - males are dark brown to black with distinctive white bands and transparent wing patches, while females are much larger and reddish-brown with lighter markings. Both sexes have fuzzy, feathery antennae and the characteristic eyespots found on many silk moths. These beautiful creatures spend most of their lives as caterpillars, then overwinter in tough, papery cocoons before emerging as adults in late spring.

idTips.label: Sexual dimorphism
idTips.description: Males look completely different from females - males are smaller, dark brown to blackish with white bands, while females are much larger and reddish-brown with cream-colored markings

idTips.label: Feathery antennae
idTips.description: Both sexes have distinctly feathery, branched antennae that feel soft and delicate to the touch - males have especially elaborate ones that look like tiny ferns

idTips.label: Wing eyespots
idTips.description: Look for small eyespot markings on the wings that shimmer slightly in sunlight, though they're more subtle than those on other silk moths

idTips.label: Cocoon appearance
idTips.description: Overwintering cocoons are tough, papery brown cases that hang from twigs like dried leaves and make a slight rattling sound if the pupa has moved inside

idTips.label: Day-flying males
idTips.description: Unlike most large moths, males are active during the day, especially in late afternoon, flying with a distinctive fluttering pattern

habitat: Look for Promethea Silkmoths in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially where their host plants grow abundantly. They favor areas with spicebush, wild cherry, tulip tree, white oak, and sassafras. You'll find them from forest edges to deep woods, particularly in areas with dappled sunlight and rich, moist soil.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from overwintering cocoons in May and June. This is peak time to spot the day-flying males and find empty cocoons still hanging from branches.
seasonality.summer: Caterpillars are actively feeding on host plants, growing larger through the summer months. Look for the distinctive larvae with their colorful warning patterns.
seasonality.fall: Mature caterpillars spin their cocoons in late summer and fall, creating the papery brown cases that will hang from trees all winter.
seasonality.winter: Pupae develop inside the tough brown cocoons hanging from deciduous trees - these are often most visible once leaves have fallen.

funFact: Promethea Silkmoths are the only moths in their entire family where males and females are active at completely different times - males fly during the day while females are nocturnal, meeting only for a brief window during early evening twilight for their romantic rendezvous.
confusionNotes: Male Prometheas are often mistaken for the poisonous Pipevine Swallowtail butterfly, which is actually intentional mimicry for protection! Remember: butterflies hold their wings vertically when resting, while moths hold theirs horizontally, and moths have feathery antennae versus the butterfly's thin, club-tipped ones.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'silkmoth,' the Promethea's silk isn't commercially valuable like that of domestic silkworms. The 'silk' refers to the strong fibers they use to construct their remarkably durable cocoons, which can withstand an entire New England winter hanging exposed on tree branches.
compareHints: Since Promethea is the only species in its genus Callosamia in our region, compare it to other giant silk moths like the Cecropia or Luna moths. Prometheas are smaller than Cecropias and lack the Cecropia's bright red, white, and black banding, while they're much more subdued in color than the pale green Luna moths with their distinctive long tails.
